subject: IDS
course_description: Highly focused courses, drawing on multiple disciplines of the humanities and social sciences; may be repeated for credit when topics vary.
course_notes: Memory creates the foundation for who we understand ourselves to be. How do memoirs, acts of narrative- and self-construction, use memory and forgetting in the creation and revision of lived meaning? How do writers navigate the lines between truth and fact? What are some of the literary strategies that make for a compelling memoir? What is the role of research in writing memoir? Addressing these and other questions, this course examines the choices memoirists make as they negotiate both memory and self-identifications such as gender, race, class, sexual orientation, geography, and religion. Readings will focus on a variety of modern memoirs (books and essays), in addition to academic articles and studies on memory. Grades will be based on attendance, occasional quizzes or short (one-page) response papers on the readings, a 6 to 7¿page memoir midterm paper, and a 6 to 7¿page oral history final paper. Please note that dropping into this course late in the add/drop/swap period will entail a great deal of catch up on reading and assignments. Because class sessions are largely organized around discussion, attendance (with one or two explained absences excepted) is vital not only to your success in the course but also to the development of our typically tight-knit cohort, one that reads and writes together while exploring our own and others' stories.
